sections.title: A pot with a name on it
sections.intro_md:
In **2015**, archaeologists digging in a coconut grove at **Keeladi**, a village about 12 km southeast of Madurai, found brick walls, drains, ring wells, dice, spindle whorls and gold beads. They also found broken pots scratched with personal names in **Tamil-Brahmi**, the oldest Tamil script: *Aathan*, *Kuviran*, *Thisan*.

In **2019** the Tamil Nadu archaeology department published a carbon date for one of the layers: about **580 BCE**. If the dating holds, people in a town on the Vaigai were writing their names on pots at roughly the time the Buddha was born, and a full urban culture existed in the far south far earlier than textbooks said.

That is Tamil Nadu in one scene. A state of **72 million** people (2011) that is also one of India's two biggest factory floors, and that argues, loudly and in public, about how old its language is. Today you will meet the temples, the poets, the film stars who became chief ministers, the dishes, and the 2026 election that broke a 59-year habit.

spotlights.name: Keeladi excavations
spotlights.when: Digs since 2015; settlement dated to about the 6th century BCE
spotlights.spot_it: Square trenches in a coconut grove, with red brick walls, terracotta ring wells and rows of broken pots.
spotlights.story_md: The first seasons, from **2014 to 2017**, were run by the Archaeological Survey of India under **K. Amarnath Ramakrishna**. In 2017 he was transferred to Assam and the ASI wound down, which many in Tamil Nadu read as politics. The state took over from 2018. Its finds run into the thousands: ivory dice, terracotta toys, iron tools, gaming pieces and a notable absence of clear religious objects. Specialists accept an early date for the site but still argue over whether the inscribed sherds sit in the same layer as the oldest sample. A heritage museum opened next to the trenches on **5 March 2023**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It moved the start of urban life in Tamil Nadu back by centuries.
spotlights.memory_hook: Keeladi: a coconut grove that turned out to be a 2,500-year-old town.

spotlights.name: Tamil-Brahmi script

where.label: Caves and pot sherds across Tamil Nadu

spotlights.when: From about the 3rd century BCE, possibly earlier
spotlights.spot_it: Short lines of angular letters cut into a cave's rock lip above stone beds, or scratched on a pot.
spotlights.story_md: Tamil-Brahmi is Brahmi adapted to Tamil sounds. Its earliest examples are carved on the drip ledges of natural caves near Madurai, where Jain monks slept on smoothed stone beds, and on pottery found from Keeladi to Egypt's Red Sea ports. A sherd inscribed in Tamil-Brahmi turned up at **Berenike**, a Roman port in Egypt, and another in Oman. The script ties the Sangam poems to real people: some names on rock match chieftains praised in the poetry. Modern Tamil letters grew out of it, through the Vatteluttu and Grantha scripts.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows Tamil was written, traded and travelled more than 2,000 years ago.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Tamil name on a pot in Egypt: the oldest Tamil travelled before Rome fell.

sections.title: The state at a glance
sections.intro_md:
Tamil Nadu is India's southeastern corner: **130,058 km²**, the 10th largest state, with a **1,076 km** coast on the Bay of Bengal and the Indian Ocean, the second longest of any state. It had **72.1 million** people in 2011 and is estimated at about 77 million now. It is split into **38 districts**, elects **234** members to its assembly and sends **39** MPs to the Lok Sabha.

Three numbers explain its weight. Its economy, about **₹31 lakh crore** in 2024 to 25, is India's second largest after Maharashtra. Almost **half its people live in towns** (48.4% in 2011), far above the national 31%. And its women have on average **1.8 children** (NFHS-5), below replacement, the demography of a middle-income country.

The state's name means 'Tamil country'. It was called **Madras State** until **14 January 1969**, and its capital was Madras until **1996**, when the city became Chennai.

spotlights.name: Chennai
spotlights.when: Founded as a trading post on 22 August 1639
spotlights.spot_it: A flat, sprawling coastal city of low buildings, long beaches, temple towers and IT parks along a south-running highway.
spotlights.story_md: On **22 August 1639** two East India Company men, **Francis Day** and **Andrew Cogan**, got a strip of sandy coast from a local Nayak governor. The date is now celebrated as Madras Day. The city that grew there became the capital of the **Madras Presidency**, which at its peak ran from Kerala to Odisha. Today about 11 million people live in greater Chennai. It makes cars, phones and software, hosts the December music season, and is the home of Tamil cinema. It also runs out of water: in **June 2019** its four main reservoirs went nearly dry.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the political, cultural and industrial centre of the Tamil world.
spotlights.memory_hook: Chennai: born on a beach in 1639, renamed in 1996, still sweating in between.

spotlights.name: Fort St George
spotlights.spot_it: A low, white colonial fort by the sea, with a tall flagstaff and a red-and-white secretariat building inside.
spotlights.story_md: Fort St George was the **first English fortress in India**, finished around 1644. Inside it stands **St Mary's Church** (1680), the oldest Anglican church east of Suez, where Robert Clive married in 1753. Elihu Yale, a governor of Madras, made a fortune here and later gave money that named **Yale University**. The fort is still in use: it houses Tamil Nadu's **Legislative Assembly and Secretariat**, so the state is governed from inside a 17th-century trading fort. India's tallest flagstaff of its day once stood on its ramparts.
spotlights.why_it_matters: British India began here, and Tamil Nadu is still run from it.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Yale fortune and a state government, both from one seaside fort.

spotlights.name: Marina Beach
spotlights.spot_it: A very wide stretch of pale sand in front of a city, crowded with families, kites and food stalls at sunset.
spotlights.story_md: The Marina runs about **6 km** from Fort St George to the Foreshore Estate, and with its southern extension it is often called the longest urban beach in India. The sand is unusually wide, up to 300 m. The rip currents are strong, so swimming is banned. It is also Tamil Nadu's political stage: memorials to **Annadurai, MGR, Karunanidhi and Jayalalithaa** line the beach, and in **January 2017** hundreds of thousands camped on it for a week to bring back jallikattu. The 2004 tsunami killed more than 200 people here.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where Chennai relaxes, mourns and protests.
spotlights.memory_hook: Chief ministers buried on the sand, and a protest that changed a law.

sections.title: Mountains, a delta and the end of India
sections.intro_md:
Tamil Nadu tilts from the **Western Ghats** in the west down to the Bay of Bengal in the east. The highest point is **Doddabetta**, 2,637 m, in the Nilgiris. Between the hills and the sea lie dry plains of red soil and palmyra palms, and the **Kaveri delta** around Thanjavur, the old rice bowl.

One quirk shapes life here. Most of India gets its rain from the southwest monsoon in June to September. Tamil Nadu sits in the rain shadow of the Ghats, so it gets nearly half its rain from the **northeast monsoon** in October to December, along with the cyclones. Water is a constant worry, and the Kaveri, shared with Karnataka, has been in court for more than a century.

The state ends at **Kanyakumari**, where three seas meet, and reaches toward Sri Lanka along the Rameswaram island chain. Its forests hold one of India's largest elephant and tiger populations.

spotlights.name: Nilgiri Mountain Railway
spotlights.when: Opened to Ooty in 1908; UNESCO World Heritage 2005
spotlights.spot_it: A small blue-and-cream train pushed uphill by a steam engine from behind, climbing through tea gardens and tunnels.
spotlights.story_md: The line climbs **46 km** from Mettupalayam to Ooty, rising from about 330 m to 2,200 m. The steepest part is so sharp, about 1 in 12, that the train uses a **rack and pinion**: a toothed rail in the middle of the track that a cog under the engine grips. The steam engine pushes from below rather than pulling, so a coupling failure cannot send carriages rolling away. The trip takes nearly **five hours** uphill, making it one of India's slowest trains, at about 10 km/h. UNESCO added it to the Mountain Railways of India in **2005**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the last working rack railways in Asia.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five hours to climb 46 km, with the engine pushing from behind.

spotlights.name: Kanyakumari
spotlights.spot_it: Two rocky islets just offshore, one with a stone memorial hall, the other with a giant standing statue of a bearded poet.
spotlights.story_md: Kanyakumari is the southern tip of mainland India, where the Bay of Bengal, the Arabian Sea and the Indian Ocean meet. In some months you can watch the sun rise and set over water from the same spot. **Swami Vivekananda** meditated on a rock offshore in **1892**; a memorial was built there in 1970. On the next rock stands the **Thiruvalluvar Statue**, unveiled on **1 January 2000**. It is **133 feet** tall, one foot for each of the 133 chapters of the poet's *Tirukkural*. A **glass-floored bridge** linking the two rocks opened in December 2024.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the symbolic end of India, and Tamil Nadu fills it with Tamil poetry.
spotlights.memory_hook: 133 feet of poet for 133 chapters of verse.

spotlights.name: Pamban bridges
spotlights.spot_it: A long, low railway bridge across turquoise sea, with a steel section in the middle that lifts to let boats through.
spotlights.story_md: From **1914** to **2022**, trains reached Rameswaram island over a **2 km** sea bridge with a middle section that split and rose like a drawbridge for ships. It survived the **1964 cyclone**, which wrecked the island's tip and swept a passenger train into the sea near Dhanushkodi. Corrosion closed it in December 2022. Its replacement, opened on **6 April 2025**, is India's first **vertical-lift sea bridge**: a 72.5 m steel span rises straight up, like a lift, to let vessels pass.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It connects India's pilgrim island to the mainland in one of its harshest marine settings.
spotlights.memory_hook: The old bridge opened like jaws; the new one goes up like a lift.

spotlights.name: Pichavaram mangroves
spotlights.spot_it: Narrow green water channels walled by mangrove roots, with rowing boats slipping between them.
spotlights.story_md: Pichavaram is one of India's largest mangrove forests, about **1,100 hectares** of islands and some **4,000 channels** between the Vellar and Coleroon estuaries. Boatmen row visitors through tunnels of roots. When the **2004 tsunami** hit this coast, villages behind the mangroves suffered much less damage than those on open beaches, a finding that pushed India to plant and protect mangroves along its coasts. The forest also feeds the prawn and fish catch that sustains nearby fishing villages.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a natural sea wall, proven in 2004.
spotlights.memory_hook: The trees that stood in front of the tsunami.

spotlights.name: Nilgiri tahr
spotlights.spot_it: A stocky brown wild goat with short curved horns, standing on steep grassy cliffs; old males have a pale saddle.
spotlights.story_md: The Nilgiri tahr lives only in the high grasslands of the southern Western Ghats, in Tamil Nadu and Kerala. It is Tamil Nadu's **state animal** and appears in Sangam poetry as *varudai*. Hunting and the planting of hills with tea, eucalyptus and wattle shrank its range. Tamil Nadu launched a dedicated **Nilgiri Tahr Project** in 2023, and its first synchronised survey in **2024** counted roughly a thousand animals in the state. Together with Kerala's Eravikulam park, the world population is in the low thousands.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the emblem of the Western Ghats' fragile grasslands.
spotlights.memory_hook: The state animal is a cliff goat that only lives on a few hilltops.

spotlights.name: Mudumalai's elephants
spotlights.spot_it: Dry teak forest with elephants bathing in a river and keepers in shorts scrubbing them down.
spotlights.story_md: Mudumalai is a tiger reserve where Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka meet, part of the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve that holds one of the largest Asian elephant populations left. At **Theppakadu**, one of Asia's oldest elephant camps, mahouts from the Kattunayakan tribe raise orphaned calves. A couple there, **Bomman and Bellie**, raised an orphan called **Raghu**. Their story became *The Elephant Whisperers*, which won the **Oscar** for best documentary short in **2023**, the first Indian production to win in that category.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows wildlife care as a family job for forest communities.
spotlights.memory_hook: An orphan elephant from the Nilgiris walked onto the Oscar stage.

spotlights.name: The Kaveri and the Grand Anicut
spotlights.when: Dam first built about the 2nd century CE
spotlights.spot_it: A wide, shallow river spreading into green paddy, with an old stone weir and round basket boats upstream.
spotlights.story_md: The Kaveri enters Tamil Nadu through the gorge at **Hogenakkal**, where boatmen ferry visitors in round **coracles**, and fans out into a delta of canals before the sea. At **Kallanai**, a weir of unhewn stone across the river is credited to the Chola king **Karikalan** around the 2nd century CE, and is often called the oldest water-diversion structure still in use. The British engineer Arthur Cotton studied it in the 19th century. The river's water has been disputed with Karnataka since the 1890s; the Supreme Court set its latest shares in **2018**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Rice, kings and lawsuits all flow from this river.
spotlights.memory_hook: A 2,000-year-old dam, and a 130-year-old quarrel.

sections.title: Three crowned kings and the poets
sections.intro_md:
The early history of Tamil Nadu is written in poetry. The **Sangam** anthologies, about **2,381 poems** by 473 named poets composed roughly between the 3rd century BCE and the 3rd century CE, describe a land ruled by three crowned kings: the **Cheras** in the west, the **Cholas** in the Kaveri delta and the **Pandyas** at Madurai, plus many hill chiefs.

Outsiders confirm the picture. Emperor **Ashoka**'s rock edicts, around 260 BCE, name the Cholas and Pandyas as independent neighbours beyond his empire. Roman coins turn up in hoards across the state, and the Roman writer Pliny grumbled that India drained the empire of gold for pepper, pearls and cloth. Much of the trade ran through Tamil ports such as Arikamedu and Korkai.

The poems sort life into two halves: ***akam***, the inner world of love, and ***puram***, the outer world of war, kings and generosity. Each landscape, from hills to seashore, has its own flower, god and mood.

spotlights.name: The Sangam anthologies
spotlights.when: About 3rd century BCE to 3rd century CE
spotlights.spot_it: Short Tamil poems that open with a landscape, a flower or an animal and turn it into a feeling.
spotlights.story_md: Tradition says the poems were judged at academies (*sangams*) in Madurai. The anthologies were nearly lost: by the 19th century they survived only on crumbling palm leaves in monasteries and private homes. The scholar **U. V. Swaminatha Iyer** spent decades from the 1880s tracking down manuscripts village by village and printing them. In one famous poem a girl says her love for a man of the hills is 'bigger than the earth, higher than the sky, deeper than the sea'. The poet **A. K. Ramanujan**'s translations brought them to world readers in the 1960s.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are among the oldest secular love and war poetry in any Indian language.
spotlights.memory_hook: Love bigger than the earth, saved from termites on palm leaves.

spotlights.name: Mamallapuram's rock-cut temples
spotlights.spot_it: Five chariot-shaped temples carved from single boulders, and a weathered granite temple standing on the beach.
spotlights.story_md: The **Pallava** kings of Kanchipuram turned their port of Mamallapuram into a stone workshop. The **Pancha Rathas** are each carved out of a single rock outcrop in the 7th century, with a life-size stone elephant beside them. The **Shore Temple**, built around **700 CE**, is one of the earliest free-standing stone temples in South India. When the **2004 tsunami** pulled the sea back, onlookers saw the remains of other structures under water, which revived old sailors' tales of seven pagodas. UNESCO listed the site in **1984**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Here South Indian builders learned to turn rock into temples.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five temples, five boulders, no blocks.

spotlights.name: Descent of the Ganges
spotlights.spot_it: A huge rock face covered with gods, people and life-size elephants, split by a natural cleft where water once ran.
spotlights.story_md: This is one of the largest open-air rock reliefs in the world, about **29 m long and 13 m high**, carved on two boulders. A natural cleft in the middle was probably fed with water from a tank above, so a real stream ran down where the sculptors put the river Ganga and its snake deities. Around it, over 100 figures crowd in: a sage standing on one leg, a family of elephants, and a famous cheeky detail, a **cat** standing in yogic penance while mice gather at its feet. Scholars still debate whether it shows Arjuna's penance or Bhagiratha bringing down the Ganga.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a masterpiece of Indian narrative sculpture.
spotlights.memory_hook: A cat pretending to meditate so the mice come close.

spotlights.name: Brihadisvara Temple, Thanjavur
spotlights.spot_it: A pyramid-shaped granite tower about 66 m tall, with a massive stone Nandi bull in a pavilion facing it.
spotlights.story_md: Built by **Rajaraja Chola I** and completed in **1010**, the 'Big Temple' was the tallest temple in India of its day. Its tower, about **66 m**, is made of granite, in a delta with no granite quarry nearby; the stone was hauled from tens of kilometres away. The top is crowned by a huge capstone, often said to weigh **80 tonnes**. Inscriptions on its walls list the temple's staff, including about 400 dancers and their addresses, and the jewels donated to it. In **2010**, its thousandth year, the government issued a commemorative stamp and coin.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the grandest statement of Chola power, still in worship after 1,000 years.
spotlights.memory_hook: A thousand-year-old granite tower in a land without granite.

spotlights.name: Rajendra Chola I and Gangaikonda Cholapuram
spotlights.spot_it: A graceful temple tower with gently curved sides, standing almost alone among fields: the remnant of a vanished capital.
spotlights.story_md: Rajaraja's son **Rajendra I** took the Chola army to the **Ganges** around 1019 to 1025 and had the defeated kings send its water back south. He founded a new capital called **Gangaikonda Cholapuram**, 'the city of the Chola who took the Ganges', and built a temple modelled on his father's. In **1025** his navy raided the **Srivijaya** empire across the Bay of Bengal in what is now Indonesia and Malaysia, a rare overseas naval expedition by an Indian king. The capital later fell to ruin; only the temple stands.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It marks the high point of Tamil sea power.
spotlights.memory_hook: He brought back the Ganges in pots and sent ships to Sumatra.

spotlights.name: Chola bronze Nataraja
spotlights.spot_it: Shiva dancing inside a ring of flames, one leg raised across his body, hair flying out, standing on a small dwarf.
spotlights.story_md: Chola bronzes were cast by the **lost-wax** method: a model in beeswax and resin is coated in clay, heated so the wax runs out, and filled with molten metal. Each mould is broken, so each piece is unique. The bronzes were made to be carried in processions, so they have holes in the base for poles. The **Nataraja**, Shiva as lord of the dance, sums up a whole philosophy: creation in one hand, destruction in another, ignorance crushed underfoot. In **2004** India gave a 2 m Nataraja to **CERN**, the particle physics lab near Geneva.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Many people know Indian art first through this one image.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Chola dance of creation, now standing at a particle physics lab.

sections.title: How Tamil Nadu became Tamil Nadu
sections.intro_md:
Under British rule the region was the core of the **Madras Presidency**, a sprawling province that included much of today's Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Karnataka. English education, missionaries and the railways created a new class of clerks and lawyers, and Brahmins, about 3% of the population, held a large share of government posts. That imbalance sparked the defining political idea of modern Tamil Nadu.

The **Justice Party** (1916) demanded jobs for non-Brahmins and in **1921** passed India's first caste-based reservation order. **Periyar**'s **Self-Respect Movement** (1925) attacked caste, ritual and the subordination of women. His followers formed the **Dravida Kazhagam**, and in **1949** C. N. Annadurai split off to found the **DMK**, which took the movement into elections.

The tipping point came in **1965**, when Hindi was due to become India's sole official language. Students rioted across the state; dozens died. Two years later the DMK swept the Congress from power. From **1967 to 2026**, every chief minister came from the DMK or its offshoot, the AIADMK.

spotlights.name: Periyar E. V. Ramasamy
spotlights.spot_it: An old man with a long white beard, black shirt and a walking stick, often seated with a hand raised.
spotlights.story_md: Born into a rich merchant family in **Erode**, Periyar was a Congress leader who quit in 1925, convinced the party would not fight caste. His **Self-Respect Movement** promoted marriages without priests, and Tamil Nadu legalised such **self-respect marriages** in 1967. He called for women's right to divorce, abortion and property decades before the law allowed them. At **Vaikom** in Kerala in 1924 he joined the protest to open temple roads to all castes. He was also a fierce atheist and a divisive figure; his statues carry the words 'there is no god'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He set the ideas that every Tamil Nadu government since 1967 has claimed.
spotlights.memory_hook: Periyar: black shirt, white beard, no priest at the wedding.

spotlights.name: C. N. Annadurai
spotlights.spot_it: A short man in a white shirt and dhoti, a shawl on his shoulder, with a broad face and a gentle smile.
spotlights.story_md: Annadurai, called **Anna** ('elder brother'), was a writer and playwright who used theatre and film to carry Dravidian ideas into villages. He founded the **DMK** in **1949** and led it to power in **1967**. In barely two years as chief minister he legalised self-respect marriages, adopted a **two-language policy** (Tamil and English, no Hindi in state schools) and renamed Madras State as **Tamil Nadu**, which took effect on 14 January 1969. He died weeks later of cancer. His funeral in February 1969 was reported to draw about 15 million people.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Both main Dravidian parties still carry his name or his face.
spotlights.memory_hook: Anna named the state, then died weeks later.

spotlights.name: K. Kamaraj and the school meal
spotlights.spot_it: A big, dark, heavy-set man in a white khadi shirt and dhoti, with a towel over one shoulder.
spotlights.story_md: Kamaraj left school around class six to work in a shop, yet as chief minister he opened thousands of schools so that, the saying goes, no child had to walk more than a few kilometres to one. He expanded **free school meals** in the 1950s so poor parents would send children to class. MGR made the scheme universal in **1982**, and in **2001** the Supreme Court ordered every state to serve cooked midday meals. In **2022** Tamil Nadu added a free **breakfast** for primary pupils. In Delhi, Kamaraj was the 'kingmaker' who chose two prime ministers, Shastri and Indira Gandhi.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's midday meal, which now feeds over 100 million children, grew from his idea.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sixth-class dropout who put lunch on every school's timetable.

sections.title: Tamil, the language that is the state
sections.intro_md:
In Tamil Nadu, language is not just how you talk. It is the reason the state exists, the core of its politics and a source of fierce pride. **Tamil** is spoken by about **88%** of the state (2011) and by roughly **80 million** people worldwide. It is an official language in **Sri Lanka** and **Singapore**, and large communities live in Malaysia, Mauritius, South Africa, Fiji, Canada and the Gulf.

In **2004** Tamil became the first language India declared **classical**, on the strength of a literature more than 2,000 years old that grew independently of Sanskrit. Its oldest surviving grammar, the ***Tolkappiyam***, may date to the last centuries BCE.

Tamil is strongly **diglossic**: the written language of books and news is quite different from everyday speech, and a Chennai street conversation would read oddly on paper. English borrowed several everyday words from it: **catamaran** (*kattumaram*, 'tied logs'), **mango** (*mangai*), **curry** (*kari*) and **cheroot**.

spotlights.name: Tirukkural
spotlights.when: Commonly dated 1st century BCE to 5th century CE
spotlights.spot_it: Two-line verses, each just seven words, often painted above the seats on Tamil Nadu government buses.
spotlights.story_md: The *Kural* by **Thiruvalluvar** has **1,330 couplets** in **133 chapters**, split into three books: virtue, wealth and love. Each couplet is exactly seven words over two lines. It names no god, king or caste, which is one reason every Tamil faith and party claims it. It has been translated into dozens of languages; an Italian Jesuit, **Constanzo Beschi**, put parts into Latin in the 1730s, and Tolstoy and Gandhi admired it. Tamil Nadu buses display a couplet, and politicians quote one in nearly every budget speech.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the moral handbook of the Tamil world.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seven words a verse, 1,330 times, and not one god named.

spotlights.name: Subramania Bharati
spotlights.spot_it: A poet in a white turban with a bold upturned moustache and a fierce, direct stare.
spotlights.story_md: Bharati wrote poems that made modern Tamil a language of freedom, women's equality and plain speech. He dreamed of a bridge to Sri Lanka and of women walking with their heads held high. Hunted by the British for his nationalist journalism, he lived in exile in French **Pondicherry** from **1908** to 1918. In 1921 he was knocked down by an elephant at the **Parthasarathy temple** in Chennai, which he used to feed; he died a few months later, aged **38**, with fewer than 20 people at his funeral. Today his songs are sung at every school function.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He turned classical Tamil into the voice of a modern nation.
spotlights.memory_hook: The poet with the moustache, struck down by the temple elephant he fed.

sections.title: Temple towers, a basilica and a dargah
sections.intro_md:
Tamil Nadu is often called the land of temples. Its **Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments** department oversees about **44,000** temples. In the 2011 census **87.6%** of people were Hindu, **6.1%** Christian and **5.9%** Muslim.

The local signature is the **gopuram**, a pyramid-shaped gateway tower covered in painted figures. From the 12th century onward these gates grew taller than the shrines inside, and in the Nayak period of the 16th and 17th centuries they became the skyline of every temple town. A gopuram is the state emblem.

Two great devotional traditions began here between the 6th and 9th centuries: the **Nayanmars**, 63 poet-saints of Shiva, and the **Alvars**, 12 poet-saints of Vishnu. They sang in Tamil rather than Sanskrit, and they helped shape the bhakti movement across India. Christianity reached the coast early: tradition holds that the apostle **Thomas** died at Mylapore in Chennai in 72 CE. Islam arrived with Arab traders on the same coast.

spotlights.name: Meenakshi Temple, Madurai
spotlights.spot_it: Fourteen towering gateways painted in candy colours, crowded with thousands of gods, demons and animals.
spotlights.story_md: The temple is dedicated to **Meenakshi**, the fish-eyed goddess, and her consort Sundareswarar (Shiva). Unusually, the goddess comes first: pilgrims worship her before him. Its **14 gopurams** are the tallest about **52 m**, and they are repainted in bright colours roughly every 12 years. The temple draws about **15,000** visitors a day, many more on festival days. Each April and May the **Chithirai festival** re-enacts the wedding of Meenakshi and Shiva, with her brother Vishnu arriving in Madurai by the Vaigai river. The whole city was laid out in concentric squares around it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the heart of Madurai and the most famous temple in Tamil Nadu.
spotlights.memory_hook: A goddess with fish eyes, worshipped before her husband.

spotlights.name: Srirangam
spotlights.spot_it: An island town where seven concentric walls ring a shrine, entered through a huge white gateway tower.
spotlights.story_md: The **Ranganathaswamy** temple sits on an island between the Kaveri and its branch the Kollidam. Its complex covers about **63 hectares** inside **seven concentric walls**, and people live, shop and run businesses within the outer rings. It is often described as the largest functioning Hindu temple in the world. The great **Rajagopuram** at the entrance was left unfinished for about 400 years and completed only in **1987**. At about **73 m**, it is one of the tallest temple towers in Asia. The reclining Vishnu inside faces south, toward Sri Lanka.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the leading shrine of the Sri Vaishnava tradition.
spotlights.memory_hook: A temple with a town inside its walls.

spotlights.name: Ramanathaswamy Temple, Rameswaram
spotlights.spot_it: An endless pillared corridor in perspective, painted ceilings and rows of carved columns disappearing into the distance.
spotlights.story_md: Rameswaram is one of the **Char Dham**, the four sacred points of Hinduism, at India's southeastern edge. The temple's outer corridors are about **1,200 m** long in total, with more than **1,200 pillars**, and are counted as the longest temple corridor in India. Pilgrims first bathe at the sea, then walk around the temple dousing themselves at **22 wells**, each said to have water of a different taste. The legend says **Rama** worshipped Shiva here after returning from Lanka, and that the chain of shoals toward Sri Lanka is the bridge his army built.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It binds the far south into an all-India pilgrimage map.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty-two wells, one wet pilgrim, a kilometre of pillars.

spotlights.name: Velankanni Basilica
spotlights.spot_it: A tall white Gothic church by the sea, packed with pilgrims, many in saffron-coloured clothes with shaved heads.
spotlights.story_md: Velankanni is called the **'Lourdes of the East'**. Local tradition tells of three miracles by the Virgin Mary, including Portuguese sailors who survived a storm in the 17th century and built a chapel where they landed. Pope John XXIII raised it to a **basilica** in **1962**. Its 11-day festival ending on **8 September** draws millions, including large numbers of Hindus. Pilgrims shave their heads, walk on their knees and offer silver models of body parts they want healed, customs borrowed from Tamil Hindu practice. The 2004 tsunami killed hundreds of pilgrims on the beach.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how Tamil Christianity took a Tamil form.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Gothic church where pilgrims shave their heads like at a Hindu temple.

spotlights.name: Nagore Dargah
spotlights.spot_it: A white shrine with five slender minarets, the tallest about 40 m, by a busy coastal town.
spotlights.story_md: The dargah is the tomb of the Sufi saint **Shahul Hamid**, who is said to have cured the Hindu king of Thanjavur. In thanks, the Maratha ruler **Pratap Singh** of Thanjavur built its tallest minaret in the 18th century. Pilgrims of all faiths come here, and Hindu families offer silver boats and cradles for safe voyages and children. The 14-day **Kanduri** festival ends with a sandalwood paste procession. The dargah's musicians and the Nagore Hanifa songs are known across the Tamil world, including in Singapore and Malaysia.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a living symbol of shared Hindu and Muslim devotion on this coast.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Sufi tomb whose tallest minaret was paid for by a Hindu king.

sections.title: Dance, drums and the December season
sections.intro_md:
Tamil Nadu's performing arts run in two streams that met only in the last century. One flowed through temples and courts: **Bharatanatyam** and **Carnatic music**, codified by court musicians at Thanjavur in the early 1800s. The other flowed through villages: the **parai** drum, the all-night street theatre of **therukoothu**, folk songs at harvest and funerals.

In the 1930s and 1940s, reformers in Madras rebuilt the temple dance for the concert stage, and the hereditary devadasi dancers who had kept it alive were pushed out by a 1947 law that banned temple dedication. That story is still argued over. Meanwhile **Chennai** became the capital of Carnatic music. Every **December and January** the city hosts the **Madras Music Season**, started by the Music Academy in 1927: thousands of concerts and dance shows in sabhas across the city, with canteens as famous as the singers.

The folk arts, long tied to caste, have been reclaimed since the 1990s by Dalit artists and colleges as art and identity.

spotlights.name: Bharatanatyam
spotlights.spot_it: A dancer in a pleated silk costume in a half-sitting stance, knees bent outward, eyes and fingers sharp, ankle bells ringing.
spotlights.story_md: Its key position is the **araimandi**, a half-squat with knees turned out, held while the feet strike rhythm. The repertoire's order, from an opening *alarippu* to a closing *tillana*, was set by four brothers at the Thanjavur court, the **Tanjore Quartet**, around 1800. Danced by devadasis as **sadir**, it was renamed Bharatanatyam in the 1930s. **Rukmini Devi Arundale**, a Brahmin theosophist, took it to the stage and founded the **Kalakshetra** school in 1936. Each hand gesture, or *mudra*, can mean a word, so a dancer can tell a whole story with her hands.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most widely performed Indian classical dance in the world.
spotlights.memory_hook: Half-sitting, knees out, telling a story with ten fingers.

spotlights.name: Carnatic music and the Thiruvaiyaru festival
spotlights.spot_it: Hundreds of musicians sitting cross-legged in rows by a river, singing the same song together.
spotlights.story_md: Carnatic music's three great composers, **Thyagaraja**, **Muthuswami Dikshitar** and **Syama Sastri**, were all born in the town of **Tiruvarur** within about 15 years of each other in the late 1700s. Thyagaraja composed hundreds of songs in Telugu, the court language of the time. Every January, on the anniversary of his death, musicians gather at his shrine by the Kaveri at **Thiruvaiyaru** and sing his five **Pancharatna** kritis together, star vocalists beside students. The Aradhana has run since the early 20th century. In the 1920s a woman, **Bangalore Nagarathnamma**, paid for the shrine and fought to let women sing there.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is how a 19th-century composer is still honoured by an entire musical world.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hundreds of voices, one song, on the banks of the Kaveri.

spotlights.name: M. S. Subbulakshmi
spotlights.spot_it: A singer in a Kanchipuram silk sari, diamond nose studs on both sides and jasmine in her hair, eyes closed as she sings.
spotlights.story_md: Born in Madurai to a devadasi family of musicians, Subbulakshmi cut her first record at about **10**. She acted in films, including *Meera* (1945), then left cinema for the concert stage. In **1966** she sang at the **United Nations General Assembly** in New York. In **1998** she became the first musician to receive the **Bharat Ratna**. Her recording of *Suprabhatam* is played at dawn in temples and homes across South India. Gandhi said he would rather hear her speak a bhajan than hear others sing it. A shade of blue silk, 'MS blue', is named after her saris.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She is the voice most of India associates with Carnatic devotion.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sari colour named after a singer: MS blue.

spotlights.name: Nadaswaram and thavil
spotlights.spot_it: A long wooden double-reed pipe with a flared bell, paired with a barrel drum struck with a stick and thimbled fingers.
spotlights.story_md: The **nadaswaram** is one of the loudest non-brass acoustic instruments in the world, built to be heard across a temple town in the open air. Over a metre long, it is made of wood from the *aacha* tree, with a reed of dried grass. It leads temple processions and every Tamil wedding: the moment the thali is tied, the band plays the fast **kettimelam** to drown out anything inauspicious. Its partner, the **thavil**, is played with a stick on one side and fingers wearing hard thimbles on the other. The best players come from hereditary families.
spotlights.why_it_matters: No Tamil wedding or festival is complete without it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Kettimelam: the drumroll that drowns out bad luck at the wedding.

spotlights.name: Parai
spotlights.spot_it: A flat frame drum slung from the shoulder, struck with two sticks of different lengths while the drummer dances.
spotlights.story_md: The **parai** is a frame drum of cow hide played with two sticks, one thick and one thin. It is among the oldest Tamil instruments, used to announce news, war, harvest and death. Because it was played at funerals by Dalit communities, it became a mark of caste stigma, and its players were often forced to drum. Since the 1990s, groups like Buddhar Kalai Kuzhu and college ensembles have reclaimed it as an art of pride, and it now opens festivals and protests. The 2017 jallikattu protests on the Marina ran to its beat.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the sound of Tamil folk life and of Dalit cultural assertion.
spotlights.memory_hook: A drum once forced on people, now chosen by them.

spotlights.name: Therukoothu
spotlights.spot_it: Actors in huge shining crowns, puffed skirts and painted faces performing under lights on a village street at night.
spotlights.story_md: Therukoothu, 'street play', is an all-night theatre drawn from the **Mahabharata**, performed by all-male troupes in the villages of northern Tamil Nadu. A storyteller called the **kattiyakaran** acts as narrator and joker, chatting with the audience. Performances often belong to festivals of **Draupadi Amman**, a goddess form of the epic's heroine, and can run for 18 nights, one for each day of the war. The style influenced modern Tamil theatre directors and filmmakers, and a Kanchipuram school has trained koothu actors since the 1990s.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is how villagers have watched the epics for centuries.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eighteen nights of war, under a streetlight, until dawn.

spotlights.name: Silambam
spotlights.spot_it: A fighter whirling a bamboo staff so fast it blurs into a circle around the body.
spotlights.story_md: Silambam is a martial art built around a **bamboo staff**, traditionally about as tall as the forehead of the person holding it. Footwork follows patterns drawn on the ground, and spinning the staff creates a defensive wall. Sangam texts mention staffs sold to foreign traders, and the art was popular among fighters who resisted British rule. Today it is taught in schools and was added to the **Khelo India** youth games. It is often performed alongside other weapons such as the curved knife and the deer-horn *maduvu*.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Tamil Nadu's living martial art.
spotlights.memory_hook: A staff as tall as your forehead, spun into a shield.

sections.title: Silk, gold leaf and bobbing dolls
sections.intro_md:
Tamil crafts grew around temples. Temples needed bronze gods for processions, silk for deities and brides, painted images for shrines and wood for chariots. Many crafts are still made in the same towns where Chola and Nayak patrons first set them up, often by hereditary families.

Tamil Nadu now holds more **Geographical Indication** tags than almost any other state, over 60, including Kanchipuram silk, Thanjavur paintings and dolls, Swamimalai bronzes and Madurai jasmine. A GI tag means only goods made in that place by that method can use the name.

The craft that ties them together is the merchant house. The **Nattukottai Chettiars** of Chettinad were bankers who financed trade from Burma to Saigon in the 19th and early 20th centuries. They brought money and materials home and spent them on mansions, tiles and temple gifts, which is why a dry corner of Sivaganga has some of India's grandest houses.

spotlights.name: Kanchipuram silk
spotlights.spot_it: A heavy, stiff silk sari with a wide contrasting border and gold zari temple-tower patterns.
spotlights.story_md: Weavers in Kanchipuram use mulberry silk, often from Karnataka, and **zari**, a silver thread dipped in gold. The signature is the **korvai** join: the border and body are woven separately in different colours and interlocked so tightly the join cannot be pulled apart. Contrasting colours, like a red body and green border, are typical. A good piece can take **two weeks to a month** on a hand loom and weigh about **2 kg**. Brides in Tamil Nadu often wear one, and the sari is passed down to daughters.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most sought-after wedding silk in South India.
spotlights.memory_hook: A border woven separately and locked on for life.

spotlights.name: Thanjavur painting
spotlights.spot_it: A plump, round-faced god on a red or green ground, framed by raised gold leaf and inlaid glass stones.
spotlights.story_md: Thanjavur painting flourished under the **Maratha** rulers of Thanjavur. Artists paint on a wooden board covered with cloth and a paste of chalk and glue, build up raised areas in relief, and then lay real **gold leaf** over them. Coloured glass or semi-precious stones are set into crowns and jewellery. The figures, often the baby Krishna, are round and calm, with large eyes. The paintings were made for prayer rooms, not palaces. Because they shine in lamplight, they look alive in a dark shrine.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is South India's best-known classical painting style.
spotlights.memory_hook: Paintings made to glitter in an oil lamp's flicker.

spotlights.name: Thanjavur bobblehead doll
spotlights.spot_it: A painted clay figure, often a dancing woman or an old couple, whose head and body keep nodding and swaying when touched.
spotlights.story_md: The *thalaiyatti bommai*, 'head-shaking doll', has a body of clay and papier-mâché on a **round weighted base**, so it rocks back upright when pushed. The head sits on a separate pivot and nods. The physics is the same as a roly-poly toy: a low centre of gravity. It is said to have been popularised in the court of **Serfoji II** of Thanjavur in the early 1800s. The dolls are a fixture of the **golu** displays that families set up on tiered steps during Navaratri.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a toy that teaches the centre of gravity.
spotlights.memory_hook: Push it over and it nods back up.

spotlights.name: Swamimalai bronze casting
spotlights.spot_it: Craftsmen in a smoky yard pouring glowing molten metal into clay moulds packed in sand.
spotlights.story_md: Swamimalai, near Kumbakonam, is where families of **sthapathis** still cast temple bronzes by the Chola **lost-wax** method. They model each figure in beeswax mixed with resin, coat it in fine clay from the bed of the **Kaveri**, then bake it so the wax runs out. Molten five-metal alloy, *panchaloha*, is poured in. Once cool, the mould is smashed, and the figure is finished by hand with chisels for weeks. Following the ancient texts, every proportion is measured in units based on the length of the figure's face.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Chola art lives on in the same river valley.
spotlights.memory_hook: Each mould is smashed, so no two gods are alike.

spotlights.name: Chettinad mansions
spotlights.spot_it: A huge house with a pillared courtyard, Burmese teak columns, coloured tiles and Belgian mirrors, often half-empty.
spotlights.story_md: The Chettiar banking families built thousands of mansions across about **73 villages** around Karaikudi. They used **Burma teak**, **Italian marble**, **Japanese tiles** and Belgian glass, all paid for by moneylending abroad. One house could have 50 rooms around a series of courtyards. The floors are often laid with **Athangudi tiles**: handmade from local earth on glass, with colour poured into patterns, and left to dry in the sun rather than fired. After the Burmese nationalisation of 1962 and the end of overseas lending, many families left; many houses are locked, and some are being sold off piece by piece.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a rare architecture paid for by Tamil overseas finance.
spotlights.memory_hook: Burma teak, Belgian glass, and tiles dried in the sun.

sections.title: Breakfast is the main event
sections.intro_md:
Tamil food runs on **rice**, **lentils**, **tamarind** and **coconut**, with curry leaves, mustard seeds and dried chillies popped in hot oil to finish almost everything. The great Tamil meal is lunch, served on a **banana leaf**, but the dishes the world knows best are breakfasts: idli, dosa, pongal and filter coffee.

Fermented batter is the quiet genius here. Rice and black gram (urad dal) are soaked, ground and left overnight, so wild yeasts and bacteria raise the batter. That makes the food lighter, easier to digest and slightly sour.

Each region adds its own. **Chettinad** is famous for fiery, roasted spice blends. **Madurai** eats late into the night, with parotta and the cold drink jigarthanda. **Kongu Nadu** in the west cooks with coconut and groundnut, **Tirunelveli** is known for a glossy wheat halwa, and the coast eats fish curries soured with tamarind. A typical Tamil meal is vegetarian, but most Tamils are not: a 2014 government sample survey found that about 97% of people aged 15 and over were not vegetarian.

spotlights.name: Idli
spotlights.when: Described in the 10th century; steamed form later
spotlights.spot_it: White, soft, flying-saucer-shaped steamed cakes with sambar and coconut chutney.
spotlights.story_md: Idli batter is two parts rice to one part urad dal, fermented overnight, then **steamed** in moulds with dimples. Early Indian texts describe an *iddalige* made only of urad dal, and the food historian **K. T. Achaya** suggested the fermented, steamed idli may have come from Indonesia, where cooks made a similar *kedli*, but this is a theory, not proven. A Chennai caterer, **M. Eniyavan**, launched **World Idli Day** on **30 March** in 2015. One of the idli's lessons is that a meal can be filling yet light: two idlis have about 120 calories.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the default Tamil breakfast and a staple across India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Steamed, not fried: the flying saucer that feeds the south.

spotlights.name: Dosa
spotlights.spot_it: A thin, golden, crisp crêpe, often rolled or folded, sometimes a metre long, with sambar and chutneys.
spotlights.story_md: Dosa uses a batter close to idli's, spread thin on a hot iron griddle. In Tamil Nadu the classic home dosa is soft and thick, not paper thin; the long crisp 'paper roast' is a restaurant show. The **masala dosa**, filled with spiced potato, is usually credited to Udupi cooks in Karnataka, and Tamils and Kannadigas still debate the dosa's birthplace. Restaurants in Chennai serve dozens of versions, from onion and ghee roast to rava. The word dosai appears in Tamil texts at least a thousand years old.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is South India's most exported dish.
spotlights.memory_hook: Soft at home, crisp and a metre long in a restaurant.

spotlights.name: Filter coffee
spotlights.spot_it: Frothy milky coffee served in a steel tumbler set inside a wide steel bowl called a dabarah.
spotlights.story_md: Tamil coffee is made in a two-part steel **filter**: hot water drips through the grounds overnight or for 15 minutes, giving a strong decoction. This is mixed with boiled milk and sugar, then poured between the **tumbler** and **dabarah** from a height to cool it and raise froth. The grounds usually blend coffee with **chicory**, a habit that spread when coffee was expensive. **Kumbakonam degree coffee** is famous; one explanation says 'degree' comes from the lactometer reading of pure milk. Coffee came to South India from Yemen, said to be smuggled in by a Sufi, Baba Budan, in the 17th century.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the Tamil household's morning ritual.
spotlights.memory_hook: The metre pour: cooled by gravity, frothed by flair.

spotlights.name: The banana leaf meal
spotlights.spot_it: A long green leaf on the floor or table, with a mound of rice and a dozen small portions laid out in a fixed order.
spotlights.story_md: In a full Tamil meal, the leaf's **tip points left** of the diner, and each item has its place: salt and pickle at the top left, vegetables along the top, rice in the middle. The meal moves through rice with **sambar**, then **rasam**, then **curd rice**, and dessert, often **payasam**, comes early. Diners eat with the right hand. At the end, folding the leaf **toward you** says you enjoyed the meal; at funerals it is folded away. The leaf is waterproof, free and compostable, and hot food releases a faint aroma from its wax.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is hospitality, sequence and recycling in one tradition.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fold it toward you: thank you for the meal.

spotlights.name: Chettinad chicken
spotlights.spot_it: A dark, glossy, spice-coated chicken curry, red-brown and fragrant with black pepper.
spotlights.story_md: Chettinad cooking is known for spice mixes **roasted and ground fresh** for each dish: black pepper, fennel, red chillies, cinnamon and two unusual ingredients, **kalpasi** (a black lichen called stone flower) and **marathi mokku** (dried kapok buds). The Chettiar families had the money and trade links to buy spices from across Asia. Their cooks also dried and preserved vegetables and meat for long journeys. Many restaurant 'Chettinad chicken' dishes outside Tamil Nadu are much hotter and simpler than home versions.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Tamil Nadu's most famous non-vegetarian cuisine.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lichen called stone flower gives it the smoky note.

spotlights.name: Jigarthanda
spotlights.spot_it: A tall glass of pale brown milk with translucent jelly at the bottom and a scoop of ice cream on top.
spotlights.story_md: Jigarthanda means 'cool heart' or 'cool liver'. It is made with reduced milk, **badam pisin** (almond gum, which swells into jelly), **nannari** syrup from Indian sarsaparilla root, and ice cream. It is the drink of Madurai's hot nights; the city is known as the one that never sleeps, with food stalls open late. Sellers near the Meenakshi temple and Famous Jigarthanda claim the recipe; nobody is sure who made it first.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a local answer to Madurai's heat.
spotlights.memory_hook: A cool heart for a city that never sleeps.

sections.title: A year of festivals
sections.intro_md:
The Tamil year begins on **14 April**, the first day of the month of Chithirai, and its festivals follow both the sun and the moon. The great one is **Pongal**, in mid-January, which thanks the sun and the cattle for the harvest. In summer, temple chariots roll through towns. In the monsoon month of Aadi, families picnic by rivers on **Aadi Perukku** to welcome the floods. In autumn comes **Navaratri**, when homes set up **golu** displays of dolls on tiered steps. In the winter month of **Margazhi**, women draw the year's largest kolams at dawn and Chennai's music season fills every hall.

Many festivals are about light and water rather than one god, and many are shared across faiths. The main Murugan festivals, **Thaipusam** and **Skanda Shashti**, are also celebrated wherever Tamils have migrated, from Malaysia to Mauritius.

spotlights.name: Thai Pongal
spotlights.spot_it: A clay pot of rice and milk boiling over on an open fire outside a house decorated with sugarcane and turmeric plants.
spotlights.story_md: Pongal runs over four days. **Bhogi** burns old things. **Thai Pongal**, the main day, is when families cook new rice with milk and jaggery in a pot outdoors, facing the sun. When the pot boils over, everyone shouts **'Pongalo Pongal'**: overflowing means plenty. **Mattu Pongal** honours cattle, whose horns are painted and garlanded. **Kaanum Pongal** is for visiting relatives and outings. The name comes from the verb *pongu*, 'to boil over'. The sweet dish is *sakkarai pongal*; the savoury breakfast is *ven pongal*.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most important secular festival in the Tamil calendar.
spotlights.memory_hook: The pot must boil over, or the year will not.

spotlights.name: Jallikattu
spotlights.spot_it: A bull charging out of a narrow gate into a crowd of young men, one of them clinging to its hump.
spotlights.story_md: During Pongal, bulls are released one by one through a narrow gate, and young men try to hold onto the **hump** for a set distance or time. The name comes from *salli kasu*, coins tied to the horns as a prize. The Supreme Court **banned** it in **2014** on animal cruelty grounds. In **January 2017**, hundreds of thousands of people occupied the **Marina** for a week; the state passed a new law within days. The Supreme Court upheld that law in **May 2023**. Each year, injuries and some deaths are reported, mostly among participants and spectators.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It became a symbol of Tamil identity against outside rule-making.
spotlights.memory_hook: A protest of a million people over a bull.

spotlights.name: Karthigai Deepam at Tiruvannamalai
spotlights.spot_it: A huge fire blazing from a cauldron on top of a lone hill, seen from a temple town lit with oil lamps below.
spotlights.story_md: Tamil homes light rows of small clay lamps on the full moon of the month of Karthigai. At **Tiruvannamalai** the festival is enormous. At dusk, a giant fire, the **Maha Deepam**, is lit in a cauldron on top of the 800 m **Annamalai** hill, fed with **several tonnes of ghee**, and stays burning for days. It can be seen from many kilometres away. Hundreds of thousands of pilgrims walk the 14 km path round the hill. Legend says Shiva appeared here as a column of fire with no end.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the oldest festivals of light in Tamil literature.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hill wearing a crown of fire.

spotlights.name: Thaipusam
spotlights.spot_it: Devotees in yellow or saffron carrying ornate arched frames on their shoulders, some with metal skewers through cheeks.
spotlights.story_md: Thaipusam honours **Murugan**, the Tamil god of war and youth, on the full moon of the month of Thai. Devotees fast, then carry a **kavadi**, a decorated frame, often with pots of milk, to his hill temples. Some pierce their tongues, cheeks or backs with hooks and spears, a vow of devotion. The great centre in India is **Palani**. But the biggest crowds now gather abroad: about a million people go to the **Batu Caves** near Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia, and the festival is a public holiday in several Malaysian states and in Mauritius.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how Tamil faith travelled with the diaspora.
spotlights.memory_hook: Murugan's biggest party is in Malaysia.

sections.title: How people live
sections.intro_md:
Tamil Nadu is one of India's most urban, most educated and most migrant-connected states, and its daily customs carry old habits into new lives. About **80%** of adults could read in 2011, against 73% nationally. Its higher education enrolment ratio is among the highest in India, about **47%** of 18 to 23 year olds against roughly 28% nationally (AISHE 2021 to 22). Women marry later and have fewer children than in most states, and hospital births are almost universal.

Yet caste still shapes marriage, land and politics, and honour killings and caste violence make headlines every year. Surveys show most Tamil marriages are still arranged within the caste.

Some customs are visible from the street. A **kolam** at the door at dawn. **Jasmine** in a woman's hair. Men in a white **veshti** folded up to the knee. And the way people address strangers as *anna* (elder brother), *akka* (elder sister) or *amma* (mother): kinship words for everyone.

spotlights.name: Kolam
spotlights.spot_it: A white geometric pattern of loops around a grid of dots, drawn in rice flour on a freshly swept and wetted doorstep.
spotlights.story_md: Every morning, women across Tamil Nadu sweep the threshold, sprinkle it with water and draw a **kolam** freehand by letting rice powder run between finger and thumb. The traditional rice flour feeds ants and birds, an act of everyday generosity. Many kolams are drawn around a grid of dots (*pulli*) with a single unbroken line looping through. Mathematicians and computer scientists, starting with **Gift Siromoney** at Madras Christian College in the 1970s, have studied them as picture languages and fractals. In Margazhi, patterns grow huge and colourful.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is daily art, maths and hospitality in one gesture.
spotlights.memory_hook: Breakfast for ants, drawn in a single endless line.

spotlights.name: Madurai jasmine
spotlights.spot_it: Strings of small, white, very fragrant flowers coiled into a woman's braid or hung from a temple stall.
spotlights.story_md: Jasmine, *malli*, is sold strung on thread and measured by the **muzham**, the length of a forearm. Madurai's variety received a **GI tag** in **2013**: it has thick petals, a long stem and a strong scent that lasts. Women wear strands in their hair daily, not only for weddings, and men buy them on the way home. Madurai's flower market trades tonnes a day, and prices can jump tenfold during festival and wedding seasons when rain cuts supply.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the scent of Tamil streets and a GI-protected farm product.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sold by the forearm, worn every day.

spotlights.name: The veshti
spotlights.spot_it: A white cotton cloth wrapped around a man's waist, often with a thin coloured border, sometimes folded up to the knee.
spotlights.story_md: The **veshti** is a white unstitched cloth about 4 m long, wrapped around the waist. Folding it up to the knee is practical when walking or working, but it is polite to let it down when meeting elders. A border in gold zari marks a formal one; a veshti in party colours shows loyalty. In **2014**, after a Chennai club refused entry to a High Court judge wearing a veshti, the state assembly passed a law making it illegal for clubs and public places to ban it. The **lungi**, a coloured, sewn tube, is the everyday version.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is both the everyday dress and the formal dress of Tamil men.
spotlights.memory_hook: A club barred a judge in a veshti, so the state changed the law.

sections.title: Film stars who ran the state
sections.intro_md:
Nowhere else in the world have film and power fused so completely. Tamil cinema, called **Kollywood** after the Chennai studio district of **Kodambakkam**, makes around 200 feature films a year. From the 1950s, the DMK used films to spread its ideas: its writers wrote screenplays mocking priests and landlords, and its stars played heroes of the poor.

The result: since 1967, almost every chief minister has come from cinema. **Annadurai** and **Karunanidhi** were screenwriters. **MGR** and **Jayalalithaa** were stars, and MGR's wife **Janaki Ramachandran**, an actress, held the post briefly in 1988. In **2026**, actor **Vijay** became the sixth person with a film career to run the state.

Fan clubs are the link. Big stars have thousands of registered clubs that organise blood drives, first-day shows and, when the star enters politics, election work. A new release by a top star can still close offices for a morning.

spotlights.name: M. G. Ramachandran (MGR)
spotlights.spot_it: A fair man in dark glasses and a white fur cap, waving from a car.
spotlights.story_md: MGR was born in **Kandy**, Sri Lanka, and grew up poor in theatre troupes. On screen he played the righteous hero who never smoked or drank. In **1967** a fellow actor, M. R. Radha, shot him in the neck; a photo of MGR in a hospital bed with a bandaged throat helped the DMK win that year. He split from the DMK in **1972**, founded the **AIADMK**, and won every election from 1977 until his death in 1987. He made the school noon meal universal in 1982. In **1988** he was given the **Bharat Ratna**, after his death.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He showed that a film hero could be a political hero.
spotlights.memory_hook: Shot in the neck, campaigned from a hospital bed, never lost again.

spotlights.name: M. Karunanidhi
spotlights.spot_it: An old man in dark glasses, a yellow shawl around his shoulders, white shirt and veshti.
spotlights.story_md: Karunanidhi wrote the dialogue for ***Parasakthi*** (**1952**), a film whose courtroom speech against hypocrisy made Sivaji Ganesan a star and caused a storm. He became DMK leader after Annadurai in **1969** and led the party for almost **50 years**. He was chief minister five times and won all **13** assembly elections he fought. He wrote screenplays, novels and poetry well into his 90s. His son **M. K. Stalin** became chief minister in 2021. When he died in **August 2018**, a court case had to be fought to let him be buried at Marina beach.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He ran the DMK longer than most people have been alive.
spotlights.memory_hook: Thirteen elections fought, thirteen won.

spotlights.name: J. Jayalalithaa
spotlights.spot_it: A woman in a green sari and a long, cape-like overcoat, her hands joined in greeting.
spotlights.story_md: Jayalalithaa acted in more than 140 films, many opposite MGR, before he drew her into the AIADMK. After his death she took over the party and became chief minister six times. Supporters called her **Amma**, 'mother', and she branded subsidies with that name: **Amma Canteens**, opened in 2013, sold idlis for **₹1**. She was convicted in a wealth case in 2014, acquitted, then lost the post again before winning in 2016. She died in office on **5 December 2016**. The Supreme Court later upheld her conviction in that case, after her death.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She built one of India's most personal political brands.
spotlights.memory_hook: A one-rupee idli, branded 'Amma'.

spotlights.name: Rajinikanth
spotlights.spot_it: A star known for his flick of sunglasses and cigarette tosses, now bald and white-bearded off-screen.
spotlights.story_md: Born **Shivaji Rao Gaikwad** in Bangalore to a Marathi family, he worked as a bus conductor before acting school. His style, sunglasses spun onto his face and cigarettes flipped into his mouth, made him the biggest star of Tamil cinema. His film *Muthu* (1995) became a hit in **Japan**, where it gained a large fan base. He announced a political party in 2020 and withdrew weeks later, citing health. His fans, called **Thalaivar** devotees, bathe his cut-outs in milk on release day.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He shows how far a star's brand can travel, even to Japan.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bus conductor who became 'Thalaivar', the leader.

spotlights.name: A. R. Rahman
spotlights.spot_it: A slight, bearded composer at a keyboard, softly spoken, often in dark clothes.
spotlights.story_md: Rahman began as a session keyboard player and jingle composer. His first film score, **Roja** (**1992**), with director Mani Ratnam, changed Indian film music with its sound design, digital production and new voices. He went on to compose for Hindi, Tamil and international films. In **2009** he won **two Oscars** for *Slumdog Millionaire*, for best score and best song, *Jai Ho*. He runs a music conservatory in Chennai, KM Music Conservatory, founded in 2008.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He took Tamil film music to the world stage.
spotlights.memory_hook: From jingles to two Oscars in one night.

sections.title: Minds the world knows
sections.intro_md:
Tamil Nadu has produced a striking number of scientists and thinkers who shaped their fields. Several came from small temple towns with good schools and a culture that prized learning, and several left, for Cambridge, Bangalore or California, to do their best work.

The state's habit of producing mathematicians, engineers and chess players is not an accident. Madras had early universities (the **University of Madras**, 1857), early science institutes such as **IIT Madras** (1959), and a large middle class for whom exams were the way up. Today Chennai is the hub of India's chess boom: more than 30 of India's grandmasters come from Tamil Nadu.

Also worth knowing: **Venki Ramakrishnan**, born in Chidambaram, shared the 2009 Nobel in Chemistry for the structure of the ribosome. **Sundar Pichai**, who grew up in Chennai, runs Google. **Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar**, nephew of C. V. Raman, won the 1983 physics Nobel for work on the life of stars.

spotlights.name: Srinivasa Ramanujan
spotlights.spot_it: A young man with a round face and intense dark eyes, in a jacket and tie, from a single famous studio portrait.
spotlights.story_md: Ramanujan, from **Kumbakonam**, taught himself mathematics from a book of formulas and failed his college exams because he ignored other subjects. While working as a clerk at the **Madras Port Trust**, he wrote in **1913** to the Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy, enclosing pages of theorems. Hardy brought him to England. In five years he produced results that mathematicians still mine today. Told that taxi number **1729** was dull, he replied that it was the smallest number expressible as the sum of two cubes in two ways. He died at **32**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the symbol of raw mathematical genius.
spotlights.memory_hook: 1729: the taxi number that was not dull.

spotlights.name: C. V. Raman
spotlights.spot_it: A man in a white turban and suit, with a calm face and wire-rimmed glasses.
spotlights.story_md: Raman was born near **Tiruchirappalli**. On a ship to Europe in 1921 he wondered why the sea is blue, and the question led to his work on how light scatters. On **28 February 1928**, in Calcutta, he found that a tiny part of scattered light changes colour: the **Raman effect**. He won the **Nobel Prize in Physics** in **1930**, the first Asian to win a Nobel in science. He was so confident that he booked tickets to Stockholm months before the announcement. India marks **National Science Day** on 28 February.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His discovery is now used in labs, hospitals and on Mars rovers.
spotlights.memory_hook: Why is the sea blue? The answer won a Nobel.

spotlights.name: A. P. J. Abdul Kalam
spotlights.spot_it: A smiling man with a silver bob haircut parted in the middle, in a dark high-collared jacket.
spotlights.story_md: Kalam was born in **Rameswaram**, the son of a boat owner, and sold newspapers as a boy. He became an aerospace engineer, led India's first satellite launch vehicle **SLV-3** (1980) and the missile programme, and played a key part in the **1998 Pokhran** nuclear tests. As **President** from 2002 to 2007 he was nicknamed the **People's President** and answered thousands of letters from students. He died in **2015** while giving a lecture to students in Shillong. His memorial in Rameswaram draws large crowds.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is India's model of the scientist from a small town.
spotlights.memory_hook: A newspaper boy from an island who became President.

spotlights.name: Viswanathan Anand
spotlights.spot_it: A man with glasses and curly hair, bent over a chess board, chin on his hand.
spotlights.story_md: Anand learned chess from his mother in Chennai and became India's **first grandmaster** in **1988**. Known as the **Lightning Kid** for his speed, he was **world champion** five times between 2000 and 2013. His success sparked India's chess boom. In **2024** another Chennai player, **D. Gukesh**, became the youngest undisputed world champion at **18**, and Chennai is home to a chess academy culture that produces a steady stream of grandmasters, including R. Praggnanandhaa.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made chess a mainstream career in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Lightning Kid who made Chennai the chess capital.

sections.title: The factory of the south
sections.intro_md:
Tamil Nadu is India's most industrialised big state. Manufacturing makes up close to a third of its economy, and it has the **largest number of factories** of any state, about one in six in India (Annual Survey of Industries). Unlike Maharashtra or Karnataka, where money concentrates in one city, Tamil Nadu's industry is spread across many towns, each with a speciality: cars in Chennai, knitwear in Tiruppur, fireworks in Sivakasi, trucks and leather around Vellore and Ambur, textiles in Coimbatore, EVs and phones in Hosur.

The Chennai area is called the **Detroit of Asia**: it makes a large share of India's cars, with plants of Hyundai, Renault-Nissan, BMW and others. In 2024 to 25 the state became India's **top exporter of electronics**, led by iPhone makers around Sriperumbudur and Hosur.

The state's social spending is unusually generous: free bus travel for women, free school breakfast and a monthly ₹1,000 to women heads of households since 2023.

spotlights.name: Sivakasi
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of colourful firecracker boxes, sky shots and sparklers stacked high in a shop, with women packing goods.
spotlights.story_md: Sivakasi makes the large majority of India's **fireworks**, plus most of its safety matches and a big share of its printing. The industry began in the **1920s**, when two local men learned match-making in Calcutta. The town's dry climate suits the work. **Nehru** called it **'Kutty Japan'**, little Japan, for its industry. It employs hundreds of thousands. But it has a grim record of **explosions** and child labour. Air-quality rules, such as a 2018 Supreme Court ban on most chemical crackers in Delhi, hit the town hard.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the hub of India's fireworks industry and its hazards.
spotlights.memory_hook: Little Japan, where Diwali is made all year round.

spotlights.name: Tiruppur
spotlights.spot_it: Streets lined with small knitting units, bales of cotton T-shirts and cloth drying on rooftops.
spotlights.story_md: Tiruppur makes much of India's cotton **knitwear** exports: T-shirts, innerwear and baby clothes for global brands. It grew from a cotton market into a cluster of thousands of small firms that each handle one step: knitting, dyeing, printing, stitching. Workers come from across India. Its growth had a cost: dyeing units poisoned the **Noyyal** river, and in **2011** the Madras High Court ordered polluting units to shut until they cleaned up, forcing the cluster to adopt zero-discharge treatment.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a model of small-firm clusters, and of pollution's price.
spotlights.memory_hook: If your T-shirt says 'Made in India', it may be from Tiruppur.

spotlights.name: Kudankulam nuclear plant
spotlights.spot_it: Two domed reactor buildings and a tall chimney by a blue sea, with wind turbines inland.
spotlights.story_md: Kudankulam is India's **largest nuclear power plant**, built with Russia. Two **1,000 MW** reactors are running, and four more are under construction. It faced long protests by fishing villages after the 2011 Fukushima disaster. The surrounding district is also one of India's windiest: the **Muppandal** wind farm nearby is among the largest in Asia, and Tamil Nadu has one of India's largest installed wind capacities.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows Tamil Nadu's energy mix: nuclear, wind and sun.
spotlights.memory_hook: Reactors on the shore, wind turbines behind them.

spotlights.name: Nilgiri tea
spotlights.spot_it: Neat rows of bright green tea bushes on rolling hills, with women picking leaves into baskets on their backs.
spotlights.story_md: Tea came to the Nilgiris in the 19th century under the British. The hills grow a bright, fragrant tea, used often in blends and for iced tea because it does not cloud when cold. Most of the tea is grown by **small farmers**, many from the **Badaga** community, who sell green leaf to factories. The industry fights low prices and labour shortages. Nilgiri orthodox tea carries a GI tag.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It keeps the hills' economy and landscape green.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tea that stays clear in ice.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
Most visitors start with the temple circuit: **Chennai**, **Mamallapuram**, **Kanchipuram**, then south to **Thanjavur**, **Madurai** and **Rameswaram**. The Kaveri delta around Kumbakonam has the highest density of great temples anywhere, and the three Great Living Chola Temples, Thanjavur, Gangaikonda Cholapuram and Darasuram, can be seen in one long day.

For cooler air, the hill stations: **Ooty** (Udhagamandalam) and **Coonoor** in the Nilgiris, and **Kodaikanal** in the Palani hills. For forts, **Gingee** and **Vellore**. For the ghostly, **Dhanushkodi**. The best season is **November to February**, after the northeast monsoon and before the heat; April and May are very hot on the plains.

spotlights.name: Thirumalai Nayakkar Mahal
spotlights.spot_it: A vast hall of giant white pillars topped with arches and a high painted dome, in a blend of Dravidian and Islamic styles.
spotlights.story_md: The palace was built in **1636** for **Thirumalai Nayak**, the greatest ruler of Madurai's Nayak dynasty. What survives is about a quarter of the original. The courtyard is ringed by pillars **about 12 m tall** and 1.2 m wide. A light and sound show tells the story of the dynasty each evening. The palace mixes Hindu and Islamic elements, like domes and arches, a style shared with other Nayak buildings.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a rare surviving royal palace in Tamil Nadu.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pillars so wide that three people cannot hug one.

spotlights.name: Airavatesvara Temple, Darasuram
spotlights.spot_it: A small, exquisitely carved temple with a chariot-shaped hall on stone wheels, and a stone staircase that rings when tapped.
spotlights.story_md: Built by **Rajaraja Chola II** in the 12th century, this temple is the third of UNESCO's Great Living Chola Temples. It is smaller than Thanjavur but more delicate, with miniature carvings so fine they show dancers' fingers. The entrance hall is shaped like a chariot pulled by horses and elephants. Its famous **musical steps** produce different notes when tapped. Its name comes from Airavata, the white elephant of Indra, who is said to have worshipped Shiva here.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the jeweller's version of Chola architecture.
spotlights.memory_hook: Stone steps that sing when you tap them.

spotlights.name: Gingee Fort
spotlights.spot_it: Massive walls linking three rocky granite hills, with a citadel on the highest peak.
spotlights.story_md: Gingee's walls join **three hills** into one fortress. Its citadel on Rajagiri hill is reached by a steep climb and a drawbridge over a chasm. The British called it the **'Troy of the East'**. It changed hands among Vijayanagara governors, the Marathas under **Shivaji** (who called it nearly impregnable), the Mughals, the French and the British. The Mughals took **eight years**, from 1690 to 1698, to capture it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the strongest forts in South India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eight years to take, three hills to hold.

spotlights.name: Dhanushkodi
spotlights.spot_it: Roofless stone ruins of a church and railway station on a thin strip of sand between two seas.
spotlights.story_md: Dhanushkodi, at the tip of Rameswaram island, was a busy town with a railway station, port and ferries to Sri Lanka, only about **25 km** across the sea from Sri Lanka's Talaimannar. On the night of **22 December 1964**, a cyclone with a storm surge wiped it out. More than **1,800** people died, including passengers on a train swept into the sea. The town was never rebuilt. A road to the very tip, **Arichal Munai**, opened in **2017**. From there the shoals called Rama's bridge stretch toward Sri Lanka.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a reminder of the coast's cyclone risk.
spotlights.memory_hook: A ghost town where a train vanished into the sea.

spotlights.name: Kodaikanal
spotlights.spot_it: A star-shaped lake ringed by pine and eucalyptus, mist rolling over green hills.
spotlights.story_md: American missionaries founded Kodaikanal in **1845** as a retreat from the plains' heat and malaria. Its star-shaped lake was created in **1863**. The hills are famous for the **Neelakurinji** shrub, which flowers once every **12 years** and turns slopes blue-violet; the last mass bloom was in **2018**. In 2001, a thermometer factory owned by Hindustan Unilever was found dumping mercury waste here; a settlement with ex-workers came in 2016, but cleanup is debated.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the 'princess of hill stations' and a case study in pollution.
spotlights.memory_hook: A flower that waits 12 years to paint the hills.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
Tamil Nadu attracts some persistent myths, from outsiders and from inside. Some are about the past, some about people.

**Myth: the Big Temple's shadow never falls on the ground at noon.** It does; guides repeat this, but photos show the shadow.

**Myth: Tamils do not speak Hindi.** Many do. Hindi is not taught as a compulsory subject in state schools, but enrolment in voluntary Hindi courses run by the Dakshina Bharat Hindi Prachar Sabha has been large for decades. The issue is compulsion, not hatred of a language.

**Myth: Tamil cuisine is vegetarian.** A government survey shows about 97% of Tamils are not vegetarian.

**Myth: all South Indians are 'Madrasis'.** The term, once used in North India for all southerners, ignores four other states with their own languages.

**Contested: Tamil is the oldest language in the world.** Tamil is among the oldest living languages with a continuous literature, but 'oldest' claims are not testable. Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions go back to at least the 3rd century BCE, and Keeladi may push this earlier.
